design_detail: Short narrative review in CMAJ (4 pages, 38 references, single author) on the pharmacology of smoked methamphetamine hydrochloride: pharmacokinetics compared with therapeutic amphetamines, mechanism of monoamine release, the role of dopamine in liking and craving, whether methamphetamine damages the brain, and medication development. No methods section; peer reviewed according to the footnote.
can_establish: How a neurochemist who studies post-mortem brain in people who used methamphetamine summarized the drug's mechanism and the state of the brain-damage question in 2008, and which primary sources support each statement.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine causes loss of dopamine terminals, cognitive impairment or any other harm in humans: the article reviews no cognitive data, gives no systematic account of the evidence, and its human neurochemical statements rest mainly on one post-mortem study from the author's laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: narrative review; no search or selection method reported.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen by the author. Human evidence on dopamine and the dopamine transporter is cited only to the author's own post-mortem study (reference 20, Moszczynska et al., 2004); none of the in vivo PET studies of the dopamine transporter in users is cited. One source is a non-peer-reviewed drug-information website (reference 9) and one is a personal communication from Health Canada.

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as pharmacokinetic comparisons from cited studies: peak plasma d-amphetamine of about 10–110 ng/mL with long-term therapeutic extended-release mixed amphetamine salts; peak plasma methamphetamine of about 50 ng/mL after a single 30 mg smoked dose in a laboratory study; blood concentrations of 15–1600 ng/mL (median 190 ng/mL) in people using methamphetamine recreationally, sampled in a police investigation; elimination half-life about 11 hours for smoked, intranasal and intravenous routes (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Therapeutic uses, 3rd paragraph).

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. The article does not raise pre-existing differences or confounding as explanations for any human finding.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. Topics covered: monoamine release, cardiovascular activation, striatal dopamine and dopamine transporter, brain structure by imaging, relapse treatment.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Brain damage' is discussed as loss of striatal dopamine nerve terminals (animal data) versus lower dopamine and dopamine-transporter levels (human post-mortem data); cognitive impairment is mentioned but not defined or measured.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported for any brain or cognitive outcome; human findings are described qualitatively (low striatal dopamine in post-mortem brain; modestly decreased striatal dopamine transporter in some users). Quantitative statements are pharmacokinetic only (see exposure).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review; no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The human neurochemical evidence is limited to the author's own post-mortem study; in vivo imaging of the dopamine transporter, including longitudinal evidence of change with abstinence, is not cited. No cognitive studies are cited although cognitive impairment is mentioned twice.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The article reports that high-dose regimens damage striatal dopamine terminals in animals; that in humans post-mortem striatal dopamine is low in people who used methamphetamine and the dopamine transporter is modestly lower in some; that whether this reflects terminal loss or has clinical consequences is debated; that there is no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage at therapeutic amphetamine doses; and that imaging data are too preliminary to define a characteristic pattern of brain abnormality.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract keeps to that uncertainty (whether low dopamine represents neuronal loss is uncertain). The body goes further in two places: it calls it reasonable to expect from animal findings that terminal damage would also occur in people exposed to some dose (Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 2nd paragraph), and it suggests that low dopamine could explain aspects of cognitive impairment, a link for which no human data are cited (Is there a role for dopamine, 1st paragraph). The statement that the crystalline form can cause more overall harm than other forms rests on pharmacokinetic reasoning and two epidemiological sources, not on comparative harm data.

timeline.event: PET follow-up of 5 users: dopamine transporter rose with protracted abstinence, which bears on the terminal-loss question this article leaves open; not cited here.

The author's post-mortem series (Moszczynska et al., 2004), the source of this article's human dopamine and transporter statements; its numbers are summarized in the encyclopedia's card for Kish et al. (2017).
A reply titled 'Limiting production of crystal meth' (CMAJ volume 179, page 558) is linked from the PMC page; not read.

London et al. (2015), narrative review reporting conflicting VMAT2 findings in users (higher in early abstinence, lower after more than 3 months, unchanged post-mortem); appraised in sc_london_2015 from this reading batch.

Critical review by the same author concluding that it is premature to say whether recreational methamphetamine does or does not damage dopamine neurones in humans (per the encyclopedia's first-pass card).

replication.where_it_stands: The author's own later review keeps the position taken here: lower striatal dopamine and transporter levels in people who used methamphetamine are established, while whether they reflect loss of dopamine terminals, and what they mean for cognition, remain unresolved. This article adds pharmacokinetic context, not evidence on either question.

funding.funder: The author's methamphetamine studies are supported by the US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse (07186) (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: Human Neurochemical Pathology Laboratory, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto. The human evidence cited comes mainly from this laboratory. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Post-mortem studies that measure several independent dopamine-terminal markers, terminal structure and nigral cell counts in the same brains of people with documented methamphetamine exposure and of matched controls, together with in vivo imaging and cognitive testing against controls and norms followed over abstinence.

Competing interests declared as none; funding stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A short narrative review with no systematic method. It is cautious where it matters most (terminal loss uncertain, imaging preliminary, no damage shown at therapeutic doses) and useful for its pharmacokinetic comparisons, but it should not be cited as evidence on cognition or brain damage; its primary sources should be.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine raises extracellular dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine by promoting release from nerve endings, apparently by moving transmitter from vesicles into the cytoplasm (via VMAT2) and reversing transport through the plasma-membrane transporter; the author states the mechanism is not completely understood.
key_findings.locator: Pharmacologic actions of methamphetamine, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular activation is attributed largely to norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve endings; the alerting action and efficacy in ADHD are said to involve, at least partly, brain norepinephrine.

Methamphetamine and amphetamine share the same mechanism of action, and a direct human comparison found similar behavioural effects and potencies (Martin et al., 1971), though some differences cannot be excluded.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Elimination half-life is about 11 hours for smoked, intranasal and intravenous methamphetamine.

Blood concentrations in people using methamphetamine recreationally (police investigation) ranged from 15 to 1600 ng/mL (median 190), against about 50 ng/mL peak after a single 30 mg smoked laboratory dose and about 10–110 ng/mL peak d-amphetamine with long-term therapeutic extended-release mixed amphetamine salts.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Study conditions and forensic measurements, reported for comparison of exposure levels only.

key_findings.finding: High-dose methamphetamine damages striatal dopamine nerve terminals in animals; there is no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage in humans taking therapeutic amphetamine doses; some people who use methamphetamine recreationally show modestly lower striatal dopamine transporter, and whether this means loss of terminals or has clinical consequences is debated.
key_findings.locator: Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author's post-mortem study found low striatal dopamine in people who used methamphetamine, taken to mean that recreational doses can deplete dopamine; low dopamine is proposed as a possible partial explanation for withdrawal dysphoria and aspects of cognitive impairment.
key_findings.locator: Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The cognitive link is a hypothesis; no cognitive data are cited.

key_findings.finding: Imaging studies have found various structural changes in some users, but the author judges the data too preliminary to say whether any specific pattern is characteristic of chronic exposure.
key_findings.locator: Does methamphetamine cause brain damage?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The brain regions and neurochemicals responsible for methamphetamine liking and the transition to craving in humans are stated to be unknown; dopamine-receptor blockers are said not to block liking, and opioid antagonists partly blocked liking, arousal and craving with amphetamine in amphetamine-dependent people in preliminary data.
key_findings.locator: Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, paragraphs 1–3

key_findings.finding: No medication was approved in Canada for methamphetamine relapse prevention; bupropion and naltrexone had very preliminary support, a sertraline trial suggested no benefit and possibly lower abstinence, and substitution with oral amphetamine had only pilot data.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that dopamine-receptor blockers do not block methamphetamine liking is attributed to clinical findings without a citation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Unverifiable from the article; needs a primary source before use.

reporting_issues.issue: Imaging evidence that methamphetamine increases striatal dopamine release is cited to reference 18, whose title describes an anatomical framework for neuropsychiatric disorders, not an imaging study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Is there a role for dopamine in methamphetamine-craving?, 1st paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: The imaging claim has no traceable primary source in this article.

reporting_issues.issue: The suggestion from rehabilitation centres that cognitive impairment reduces programme retention is cited to reference 20, a post-mortem neurochemistry study by its title.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Treatment of methamphetamine addiction, 2nd paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Apparent citation mismatch; the clinical claim is unsupported here.

reporting_issues.issue: A recreational dose figure is sourced partly to a non-peer-reviewed drug-information website (reference 9). The encyclopedia does not reproduce it.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Therapeutic uses of methamphetamine and amphetamine, 3rd paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Source quality; not usable as evidence.
